reason: The pancreatic sensing cells are positioned to respond to the glucose-rich blood after a meal.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will detect the elevated glucose and initiate a hormonal response.

effect: The glucose-rich blood first had to be incorporated into the body; I can now try the pancreatic sensing cells on that state.
reaction: I was surprised the direct sensing-cell pairing was not accepted, though the automatic combination advanced the model.
reason: The body now has rising blood glucose, making the pancreatic sensing cells the logical next connection.
expectation: The pancreas will respond to the rising glucose with a hormonal signal.

effect: The pancreatic beta cells release insulin into the blood, with routes toward muscle and liver.
reaction: The inset makes the hormonal connection clear.
reason: The insulin route points toward skeletal muscle, making it a likely next target.
expectation: Insulin will promote glucose uptake by muscle.

effect: Insulin helped muscle take up glucose, and the new goal shifts attention to the period between meals.
reaction: The later inset makes the reduced insulin response clear.
reason: Time between meals should move the body into the situation described by the new goal.

choice.combine: Body taking up glucose into muscle

expectation: Glucose supply from the gut will taper as tissues continue using it, prompting a between-meal response.

effect: Blood glucose is falling between meals while liver glycogen remains available.
reaction: The retained glycogen suggests a clear next route.
reason: Pancreatic sensing cells previously detected rising glucose and may also respond to its fall.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will respond to falling glucose with a signal that helps make stored fuel available.

alternatives.reason: The liver's stored glycogen is another plausible next step, but a pancreatic signal may come first.

effect: Falling glucose prompted pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon, with its blood route leading toward the liver.
reaction: The contrast with beta-cell insulin release is clear.
reason: The glucagon route points to the liver, where glycogen is available.
expectation: Glucagon will stimulate the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood.

effect: The liver broke down glycogen and released glucose; as blood glucose rose, glucagon release decreased, completing the feedback example and the goals.
reaction: The sequential insets make the between-meal feedback satisfying to follow.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting glucagon to liver glycogen was most worthwhile: the planned sequence links the hormone to glucose release and reduced subsequent signalling.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial attempt to pair glucose-rich blood directly with pancreatic sensing cells was less informative than the later hormone steps, although compatibility feedback advanced the body model.

surprise.text: The direct pairing was not accepted; the glucose first had to be incorporated into the body. The automatic combination nevertheless made progress.

arbitrary.text: That initial ordering felt somewhat arbitrary: the sensing cells were already pictured beside blood, so the need to combine the blood with the body first was not obvious.

continue.text: Yes. I would be interested in another chapter that connects familiar biology to whole-body feedback as clearly as the insulin and glucagon sequences did.
